name: Frauded vs unfrauded rating

lead: On looksmaxxing forums, a frauded photo is one taken with favourable angle, lighting, lens distance, expression or editing, while an unfrauded photo shows the face neutrally, the way others see it day to day. Rating threads often ask posters to supply unfrauded pictures so that feedback reflects their ordinary appearance.

The payoff is a clearer baseline. Members who post neutral photos typically receive comments on skin, hair, eye area or facial hair, and then use that to choose what to work on. Frauding itself is also discussed as a skill, since angle and lighting choices change how a face reads in photos.

paras: Posters upload front-facing and side photos in even light without squinting, tilting or filters, and sometimes put them beside their best photo to compare. Others reply with ratings and suggestions such as skincare, a different hairstyle or grooming changes. Some users also discuss deliberate frauding for dating-app or social photos.

Ratings come from anonymous forum members and vary widely, and some threads are blunt in tone. Users report that comparing frauded and unfrauded images can be discouraging, and posting face photos publicly carries ordinary privacy considerations.

angle.text: Unfrauded threads give members a baseline of how they look in ordinary conditions. Feedback then guides changes such as skincare or a new hairstyle. Frauding, in contrast, is used to present the best version of a face in photos.

lead: Frauded versus unfrauded rating is a convention in looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org. A frauded photo is one in which angle, lighting, lens distance, expression or editing make the face look better than it usually does; an unfrauded photo is a neutral image meant to represent how the person looks in daily life.[1][2] The verb 'frauding' describes the act of presenting oneself in flattering conditions, and 'getting caught frauding' describes the moment the difference is noticed.[3]

The practice helps people improve their looks by giving them a realistic baseline. Posters who request ratings on unfrauded pictures say they want feedback on how they look every day rather than at their best, and replies often point to specific things to change, such as skin, hairstyle, eye area or facial hair.[1][4] One user who posted neutral photos listed planned changes including clearer skin, a better-fitting hairstyle and an improved eye area.[4] The flip side, frauding, is discussed as a way to look better in photos and on dating apps, including through angle choice and, for height, posture and footwear.[5][6]

The terms come from the same community vocabulary that Wikipedia traces to incel-era message boards of the 2010s and to TikTok from the early 2020s, where looksmaxxing was often framed as self-improvement and then drew coverage in The Guardian, the BBC, The New York Times and others.[6]

No published study uses the words frauded or unfrauded, but psychology and surgery research bears on the underlying question of how much photos differ from a face in person. Studies report that photographs of the same person can vary widely in rated attractiveness, and that camera distance changes how a face is perceived.[7][7][7]

paras: In rating threads, members post photographs and ask others to score them. A frauded picture uses flattering conditions; an unfrauded one is presented as an honest representation. One thread opens with the poster saying it is fair to show what they realistically look like daily and be rated against the flattering version.[1]

Other threads apply the idea to specific features, such as unfrauded side profiles, or to the unedited appearance of famous people. In one thread on actors and models filmed in harsh light at a film festival, the poster argued that skin looked much poorer than in edited images and said this motivated their own skincare work with tretinoin; another user replied that celebrities are mostly above average rather than exceptional.[2]

Looksmaxxing vocabulary grew out of message boards such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net in the 2010s and moved to mainstream platforms in the early 2020s, according to sources summarised on Wikipedia.[6] 'Fraud' as forum slang means a flattering misrepresentation of one's appearance, and the family of terms includes heightfraud (appearing taller than one is), 'frauded' photos and 'unfrauded' ones.[5][8]

Thread titles on looksmax.org show the range of use: requests for an 'unfrauded side profile', rating requests labelled with a frauded or unfrauded picture, a long guide on height frauding written by a user who describes doing it for two years, a thread on eyebags 'ruining my frauded eye area', and threads asking what members would give to be 'permanently frauded'.[8][5][9][10]

A common pattern is that a poster shares a frauded picture, other members ask for neutral photos, and the poster follows up with front-facing and side images taken without squinting, tilting or filters. Titles such as 'unfrauded no squint no angle' and 'completely unfrauded pic of me' show posters volunteering the neutral conditions up front.[11] Replies range from short rating labels to suggestions on grooming, hair and skin.[4]

A looksmax.org thread titled 'getting caught frauding is only social suicide if your unfrauded self is not good enough' shows the community discussing the social stakes: the claim is that being found out matters mainly when the everyday appearance falls short.[3]

Requests for unfrauded pictures function as a norm for getting useful feedback. Posters sometimes add disclaimers about their photos, for example clarifying that a visible asymmetry is only the moment of the photo rather than a condition.[1] Replies range from short rating labels to suggestions on grooming, hair and skin.[4]

Frauding is also discussed as a deliberate practice, including angle choice, lighting and, in height contexts, footwear and posture. Forum users debate whether being found out is socially costly, with some arguing it matters only if the unfrauded appearance falls short.

Jenkins and colleagues (Cognition, 2011) examined photos of the same faces and reported that within-person variability is often very large compared to the differences between people; unfamiliar viewers often judged photos of one person to be different people, and in one experiment variability in attractiveness within a person exceeded that between persons.[7]

Bryan, Perona and Adolphs (PLoS ONE, 2012) found that photos taken from within personal space produced lower ratings of trustworthiness, competence and attractiveness than photos taken from farther away, an effect that held across multiple studies controlling for image size, expression and lighting.[7]

Ward and colleagues (JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery, 2018) published a paper titled 'Nasal Distortion in Short-Distance Photographs: The Selfie Effect', and a 2022 review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal Open Forum states that current smartphones distort patients' perceptions of their appearance.[7][7] These studies are about photography generally; they do not address looksmaxxing ratings specifically.

lore.intro: Members use the terms to separate flattering photos from everyday appearance and often ask for brutal honesty in ratings.[1][4]
